body.value: Summary of the introduction to chapter 2 in the *Bhagavadgītābhāṣya*: the chapter sets out Sāṅkhya — knowledge of the imperishable self — and only then turns to action. On this reading the teaching of action is preparatory: action performed without claim on its results purifies the mind, and it is knowledge (*jñāna*) that liberates. The order of the chapter is itself the argument.

Summary of Śaṅkara on 2.47: *adhikāra* — entitlement — extends to action and not to its fruit. The verse is addressed to one not yet qualified for the path of knowledge; renouncing the claim on results is what makes the mind fit for that path. The verse licenses action, but as preparation, not as the end.

Summary of Tilak, *Gītā Rahasya* (1915): the renunciation commanded here is of the *claim on the fruit*, not of the action. Read as a whole the Gītā is a summons to act in the world — Arjuna is told to fight, not to withdraw — and the reading that makes it a manual of renunciation reverses its plain sense. The Gītā's final teaching is *karmayoga*: energetic action, performed without attachment to result.

Summary of Gandhi, *Anāsakti Yoga* (1929): non-attachment to results is not a licence for any action whatever. One who has truly surrendered the fruit cannot act in anger or from self-interest, and so the verse carries *ahiṃsā* inside it. The activist reading is accepted as far as it goes — the Gītā does command action — but a reading that makes detachment compatible with violence has kept the letter and lost the discipline.

*karmaṇi eva adhikāraḥ te* — sandhi-joined in the written form. **adhikāra**: entitlement, jurisdiction, qualification to undertake something. A technical term of Mīmāṃsā ritual law, where it names who is eligible to perform a rite. The word denies a *claim*, not an outcome — which is the hinge every commentator in this stack turns on.

**Machine-authored. Not a commentary.**

Observation from the three layers supplied: all three commentators accept that *adhikāra* denies a claim rather than an outcome, and all three then disagree about what a person is therefore free to do. Śaṅkara treats the freedom as freedom *from* the world, Tilak as freedom *for* action in it, Gandhi as freedom constrained by the character the discipline produces.

The verse itself supplies no scope marker — nothing in the Sanskrit says whether the release from claim applies to a monastic or a soldier. The commentators are not reading different words; they are supplying different premises about who the verse addresses. That gap in the text is where the whole 1,200-year argument sits.

body.value: If Gandhi is right that the discipline changes what you are able to do, then the verse is not a rule at all — it is a description of a person. Does any of the three read it that way? Come back to this.

習，鳥數飛也。學之不已，如鳥數飛也。

(*xí*: a bird beating its wings again and again. To learn without ceasing is like a bird flying repeatedly.)

One character, glossed once — and for six centuries every examination candidate in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam learned that 習 means *practice repeated until it becomes flight*, not *review*.

citation: 朱熹, 論語集注, 學而第一

Summary of Ibn Kathīr on the *ḥurūf muqaṭṭaʿāt*, the disconnected letters opening this sūra: he records a spread of positions rather than settling one. Among them — that these letters belong to the *mutashābihāt*, whose meaning is known to God alone; that they are names or attributes of God; that they open the sūra to arrest the listener; and that they demonstrate the challenge of the Qur'ān, since it is composed of the same letters the Arabs themselves use.

The commentary here is *about three letters*. No system that can only annotate whole verses can represent it.

citation: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, opening of Sūrat al-Baqara

body.value: Letter-granularity test: a note anchored to the middle letter alone. Which of the positions Ibn Kathīr reports would even permit a question about one letter in isolation?

Summary of *Bereshit Rabbah* 1:10: why does the Torah open with *bet* rather than *alef*, the first letter? Because the shape of *bet* is closed on three sides and open only forward — teaching that one does not ask what is above, what is below, what came before; only what is from this point onward.

The reading is of the **shape of one letter**. Note that the span covers three codepoints — the consonant and its two combining marks — because splitting them would break the rendering and, in this tradition, the text.

Scribal apparatus, not exegesis: this *bet* is one of the *litterae majusculae* — written oversized in the scribal tradition. A plain Unicode edition cannot carry that information at all, which is why scribal features are a `variant` layer over the text rather than an attempt to encode them in it.
